title: The Wheel That Turns in the Heavens Without Cleaving Them
arc: A questioner asks how the Wheel can turn within the heavens stretched from the winds down to the earth without piercing or mingling with them; the answer is that the heavens are pneumatic, and so — like a ship whose prow parts the lions of the deep but leaves no track behind, and like a bird whose flight cuts no visible road through the air — the cyclic motion of purification passes through the heavens without dividing them or being divided by them.
reading:
This chapter answers a question about the structural relation between two cosmic realities that occupy the same space: the Wheel — the cyclic process of purification turning in the heavens — and the heavens themselves, which are stretched as the Five Wells / summonses from the winds down to the earth. The questioner is troubled by a seeming contradiction. If the Wheel turns ceaselessly within the heavens, why does its motion not pierce them, and why do the heavens, in turn, not mingle inward with the Wheel as it courses?

The teacher's answer rests entirely on the discrete-degree distinction between the spiritual and the natural. The heavens cause no cleaving and suffer no cleaving "since they are spiritual" (ⲍⲙ̄ⲡⲛⲉⲩⲙⲁⲧⲓⲕⲟⲛ ⲛⲉ). Spiritual substances do not mingle with one another the way natural bodies mingle. Two natural things sharing a place must displace, pierce, and leave a wake; two spiritual things, or a spiritual and its proper motion, can interpenetrate without confusion. This is the principle the chapter is teaching, and the rest of the text supplies two correspondential pictures to make it visible.

The first picture is the ship and the lions. A ship moving through the sea has a figurehead set at the head, at the front of the prow, which "cleaves the lions" — that is, parts the surging waters as if they were dominating beasts — casting them to this side and to that. Yet at every hour, as soon as the prow has passed, the lions are joined with one another again upon the head of the ship, and the path of the ship "reveals itself in the midst of the lions" only momentarily before closing up. Read in correspondence, the lions are the dominions of the natural — the sea's surging powers as they answer to the ruling forces in the natural mind. The ship is the doctrinal vessel, the carrier of truth across the receptive depth. Its passage is real, but it leaves no abiding division in what it parts; the parted natural rejoins itself at once.

The second picture lifts the same lesson into a higher medium. A bird ascending out of the air leaves no track: "his path does not reveal itself in the air," unlike the visible road that men leave behind them when they walk on the earth under the sun. Air, the medium of thought and perception, does not retain the wake of what passes through it; only the hardened earth, the lowest natural, holds a footprint. The bird here stands for thought moving freely through the perceptive medium, and the contrast with men walking on the sunlit earth marks the difference between motion in a spiritual medium and motion in an ultimate one.

Both analogies converge on the same conclusion: "Thus likewise is this of the Wheel; it turns within the heavens and the air; the Wheel does not cleave the heavens, nor do the heavens mingle inward with the Wheel." The cyclic process of purification operates in, through, and upon the heavenly states without disturbing their order, because the heavens belong to a discrete degree above the kind of substance that can be torn or stained by motion. Influx descends, the Wheel turns, the summonses come down from the winds to the earth — and yet the spiritual order remains itself, untorn, unmingled.

The deeper teaching is reassurance about how the Lord's regenerative operation actually works. The wheeling of natural states under spiritual influence does not damage the heavens it passes through; the heavens are not split open by the soul's purification, nor do they confusedly run together with the cycle that carries her. Spiritual realities admit motion without admitting injury. What looks from below like cleaving and mingling — the visible wake left in the sea, the road pressed into the earth — is a feature of the natural alone. In the spiritual degree, the path closes behind the ship, the bird leaves the air whole, and the Wheel turns within heavens that remain undivided.

(The chapter's title, as transmitted, mentions rain mixing with the elements; the surviving text addresses the Wheel and the heavens. The principle is the same in either register — that spiritual influxes pass through their proper media without violent mingling — but the rain-and-elements segment itself is not preserved in the lines we have.)
